source.title: Scaling and Transferability of Annealing Strategies in Large Language Model Training
source.authors: Siqi Wang; Zheng-Yu Chen; Teng Xiao; Zhe-Qi Lv; Jin-Luan Yang; Xun-Liang Cai; Jin-Gang Wang; Xiaomeng Li

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses prior scaling-law formulations as a basis for a new training-loss model incorporating learning-rate and annealing terms. Its experiments concern training-loss curves and annealing strategies, not the held-out pretraining-loss claims or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation specified here.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on training-loss curves, including fitting across model sizes and predicting curves across schedulers. Those results are recorded as findings about related training-loss behavior, not as measurements of the versions, which specify held-out pretraining loss or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Annealing-ratio results concern a different scheduling choice, not the parameter/token split. Values used to estimate optimal batch sizes or fit parameters are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The paper builds a training-loss-curve formula on Kaplan/Hoffmann-style power-law terms and reports only how well its own formula fits (MAPE). The fits cover learning-rate schedules, batch sizes and annealing ratios. The model-size fits (r1, r2) do include a power-law term in N, but they score the composite formula, not whether loss scales as a power law. They also span only about 20x in parameters (47.7M–936.3M Dense; 183M–1.45B MoE), not several orders of magnitude. There is no compute-optimal allocation, shape ablation, downstream evaluation or test of fit-dependence of the original laws.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that training steps track loss curves better than tokens when batch size exceeds Bopt. They find that a forward-effect plus annealing-momentum plus model-size formula predicts training-loss curves across sizes, batch sizes and schedulers. They also find that the optimal WSD annealing ratio is transferable and predictable (power laws in max LR and steps; stable across sizes and datasets), within Dense or MoE separately.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes a training-loss formulation with step-based learning-rate and annealing-momentum terms, and studies WSD annealing choices. It does not apply the original held-out scaling-law measurement or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports differences in training-loss curves with batch size and scheduler, and annealing-ratio relationships with maximum learning rate, model size, dataset, and training steps.

fits_no_version.finding: Training-loss curves across model sizes, batch sizes and schedulers are fitted by a forward-momentum formula with MAPE under about 2%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss trajectories under different LR schedules can be modeled with an LR-integral power term plus an annealing-momentum term.

fits_no_version.finding: Step-based loss curves converge across batch sizes above an estimated Bopt, and Bopt is fitted as a power law in training loss (Eq. 11).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal batch size scales as a power of target loss, and step-based tracking is batch-invariant above Bopt.

fits_no_version.finding: The optimal WSD annealing ratio follows power laws in max LR (Eq. 13) and in training steps (exponent about -0.946 for 1B MoE). It is stable across model sizes and across training vs validation sets (Figs 5–8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The optimal annealing ratio is transferable across model sizes and scales as a power of max LR and of total steps.

record.problems: The reported model-size fitting errors are aggregate values; the main comparisons are limited to the tested Dense and MoE configurations and training-loss curves. The paper states experiments span up to 7B parameters and leaves 10B+ models and broader schedulers for future work. It does not report a test of held-out pretraining-loss scaling or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.rows_left_out: Annealing-ratio results across maximum learning rates, model sizes, datasets, and training steps (Figures 5–8) were not extracted as rows because they concern the schedule's annealing ratio, not any claim version's loss scaling or compute-optimal parameter/token split. ASMT versus CMMT fitting comparisons (Tables 5–7) were also omitted as comparisons of the paper's proposed fitting method rather than results measuring the specified claim.

untested.parts: Power-law loss in N, D or C over several orders of magnitude. Only a composite-formula fit over about 20x in parameters is reported.
Extrapolation from small runs to much larger runs. The abstract's claim that small models are proxies concerns the annealing ratio, not loss.
Effect of shape at a fixed parameter count.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer.
Downstream task performance. MMLU etc. are used only as validation loss sets for the annealing ratio.
Dependence of the original laws' exponents and allocation on fitting choices. The paper shows only that the loss trajectory depends on schedule and batch size, which its own formula models.

record.verdict_notes: I keep the reader's T4 classification. The 'Observation 1' statement of a power-law dependence on model size is asserted from the paper's own composite fit over a narrow size range. Training on The Pile is likely single-pass, so training loss roughly equals held-out loss, but this does not change the verdict. Tables 5–7 are method comparisons (ASMT vs CMMT) and are correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute; the reported curves are training-loss curves.
Prediction of held-out loss for runs orders of magnitude larger from fits on small runs; the paper reports training-loss-curve fitting and scheduler transfer, not this test.
Compute-optimal parameter and token counts at fixed compute.
Controlled comparisons of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer regimes as specified in the version.
Whether the original scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal split vary with fitting choices, or whether the original curves bend away from a single power law.

relation.reason: Established scaling laws supply the predictor's model-size and forward-effect terms; the reported results assess the proposed formula and annealing policies rather than a listed claim version.

tranche.reason: The paper incorporates established power-law terms into its own training-loss predictor and evaluates fitting and scheduler transfer. It does not test held-out loss scaling over several orders of magnitude, larger-run extrapolation over such ranges, or setup-dependent scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation.

source_check.notes: Table 1 reports r5–r10 in percent. Internal source discrepancies: the main text includes a 100M MoE absent from architecture Table 3; Figure 3 gives Dense LR 6e-4 while the batch-fitting appendix gives 5e-5; the model-size appendix additionally includes Dense 100M.
